items.stem: A report on low voter turnout among young people was planned as Introduction 8%, Literature review and context 22%, Methodology 10%, Analysis and evaluation of perspectives 48%, Conclusion and reflection 12% of 4,800 words. The draft sections contain Introduction 234, Literature review and context 1,056, Methodology 330, Analysis and evaluation of perspectives 2,254, Conclusion and reflection 526 words. Calculate the draft total and how many words must be cut, if any, to meet the 5,000-word limit. Identify the section furthest over its plan.
items.answer: Draft total = 4,400 words; within the limit. No section is over its planned length.
items.markingKey: 1 mark total; 1 mark words to cut; 1 mark section identified [3]

items.stem: A report on the spread of online disinformation during elections was planned as Introduction 10%, Literature review and context 25%, Methodology 10%, Analysis and evaluation of perspectives 45%, Conclusion and reflection 10% of 4,800 words. The draft sections contain Introduction 330, Literature review and context 1,450, Methodology 430, Analysis and evaluation of perspectives 2,560, Conclusion and reflection 430 words. Calculate the draft total and how many words must be cut, if any, to meet the 5,000-word limit. Identify the section furthest over its plan. Explain why the analysis and evaluation section should normally be the largest.
items.answer: Draft total = 5,200 words; cut 200 words. Furthest over plan: Analysis and evaluation of perspectives (+400). Most marks reward analysis, evaluation of perspectives and evidence, and a supported judgement, so space should go there rather than to description.
items.markingKey: 1 mark total; 1 mark words to cut; 1 mark section identified; 1 mark marks for analysis/evaluation; 1 mark avoid description [5]

items.stem: Tomás argues that following a standard report structure limits the quality of independent research on issues such as lowering the voting age to 16. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence.
items.answer: For: A fixed template can encourage box-ticking rather than original thinking. Some questions suit a thematic rather than sectional structure. Against: A clear structure helps readers follow a long, complex argument. Conventions such as a methodology section make the research transparent and checkable. Judgement: Structure supports quality when adapted to the question; the argument, not the template, should drive organisation.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: A student’s report on “Should the permanent members of the UN Security Council lose their veto power?” presents the perspective of a human rights NGO (calls for veto restraint in cases of mass atrocity) in Section 2 and of the African Union (the Ezulwini Consensus) (demands two permanent seats with veto power for Africa) in Section 3, then concludes in one sentence that “both sides have good points”. Explain how the student should use evidence quality to decide between the perspectives.
items.answer: Prefer the perspective supported by more credible, representative evidence (e.g. Russia has vetoed draft resolutions on the war in Syria many times since 2011), while noting vested interests (it focuses on protecting civilians; Africa has no permanent seat although many Council items concern African conflicts).
items.markingKey: 1 mark credibility; 1 mark vested interest [2]

items.stem: A student’s report on “Should the voting age be lowered to 16?” presents the perspective of a conservative columnist (opposes lowering the age) in Section 2 and of a student union (supports voting at 16) in Section 3, then concludes in one sentence that “both sides have good points”. (a) Explain why this is not a sustained argument. (b) Explain how the student should use evidence quality to decide between the perspectives.
items.answer: (a) The perspectives are described separately; there is no line of reasoning developed across the sections and no judgement. (b) Prefer the perspective supported by more credible, representative evidence (e.g. after Austria lowered the voting age to 16 in 2007, studies found that 16- and 17-year-olds turned out at rates similar to slightly older first-time voters), while noting vested interests (she believes adulthood and full rights should start at 18; its members are directly affected).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark separate description; 1 mark no developing line/judgement [2] (b) 1 mark credibility; 1 mark vested interest [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that upstream countries should agree dam operations with downstream neighbours? Consider different perspectives in your answer. You may wish to consider: the quality of the evidence; the perspective of the government of Egypt; the perspective of the government of Ethiopia.
items.answer: For: Downstream countries depend on the river for drinking water and farming. Agreed rules reduce the risk of conflict. The Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan (1960) has survived several wars. Against: Upstream countries have the right to use resources on their own territory. The argument assumes that countries will keep to an agreement once it is signed. Judgement: A sustained answer weighs the evidence and reaches a qualified judgement (response to objection: international water law also requires them not to cause significant harm to others).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. items.stem: A report’s conclusion reads: “In conclusion, this report has proved conclusively that every government should publish all public contracts online; no reasonable person could disagree.” What is the main weakness?
options: It does not answer the question
It introduces new evidence in the conclusion
It contradicts the analysis in the report
items.answer: It overstates certainty
items.markingKey: It overstates certainty. [1]

items.stem: A student’s report on “Should social media companies be legally responsible for false political content on their platforms?” presents the perspective of a press freedom organisation (warns against laws that let governments define “fake news”) in Section 2 and of an electoral commission (wants transparency rules for online political adverts) in Section 3, then concludes in one sentence that “both sides have good points”. (a) Write a supported final judgement. (b) Explain how the student should use evidence quality to decide between the perspectives.
items.answer: (a) On balance, this report concludes that social media companies should be legally responsible for false political content, because false political content can change how people vote and the evidence suggests that platforms have both the power and the incentive to shape elections; however, this holds only if companies are able to tell reliably which political claims are false, and the concern that this would turn private companies into censors of political speech remains significant. (b) Prefer the perspective supported by more credible, representative evidence (e.g. the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal showed that data from millions of Facebook users had been harvested for political targeting), while noting vested interests (such laws have been used to jail journalists; it is responsible for fair elections).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark clear answer; 1 mark supported reason; 1 mark qualification [3] (b) 1 mark credibility; 1 mark vested interest [2]

items.stem: A 4,800-word report on the under-representation of women in parliaments is planned as: Introduction 10%, Literature review and context 18%, Methodology 12%, Analysis and evaluation of perspectives 50%, Conclusion and reflection 10%. How many words are planned for the analysis and evaluation of perspectives?
items.answer: 2,400 words

items.stem: “Following a standard report structure limits the quality of independent research on issues such as reform of the UN Security Council.” To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: A fixed template can encourage box-ticking rather than original thinking. Some questions suit a thematic rather than sectional structure. Against: A clear structure helps readers follow a long, complex argument. Conventions such as a methodology section make the research transparent and checkable. Judgement: Structure supports quality when adapted to the question; the argument, not the template, should drive organisation.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a reasoned position against the report’s line of argument, which must be considered and answered”?
items.answer: Counter-argument
items.markingKey: Counter-argument: a reasoned position against the report’s line of argument, which must be considered and answered. [1]

items.stem: A report argues that upstream countries should agree dam operations with downstream neighbours. Explain how dealing with the counter-argument that upstream countries have the right to use resources on their own territory can strengthen the report’s argument.
items.answer: It shows the alternative perspective has been considered; answering it (e.g. international water law also requires them not to cause significant harm to others) removes an objection, and acknowledging what cannot be answered leads to a more credible, qualified judgement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark shows balance; 1 mark answering removes objection; 1 mark qualification increases credibility [3]

items.stem: A student’s report on “How effective are anti-corruption agencies at reducing corruption in government contracts?” presents the perspective of a government minister accused of corruption (claims the investigation is politically motivated) in Section 2 and of a business association (supports simpler procurement rules) in Section 3, then concludes in one sentence that “both sides have good points”. Explain how the student should use evidence quality to decide between the perspectives.
items.answer: Prefer the perspective supported by more credible, representative evidence (e.g. after Ukraine introduced its ProZorro e-procurement system in 2016, many observers reported savings on public purchases), while noting vested interests (he wants to protect his reputation and position; complex rules raise costs for its members).
items.markingKey: 1 mark credibility; 1 mark vested interest [2]

items.stem: A student’s report on “How effective are anti-corruption agencies at reducing corruption in government contracts?” presents the perspective of a government minister accused of corruption (claims the investigation is politically motivated) in Section 2 and of Transparency International (campaigns for open contracting and stronger enforcement) in Section 3, then concludes in one sentence that “both sides have good points”. (a) Explain why this is not a sustained argument. (b) Suggest how the student could compare the perspectives directly.
items.answer: (a) The perspectives are described separately; there is no line of reasoning developed across the sections and no judgement. (b) Organise by criteria (effectiveness, rights, cost), weighing each perspective’s reasoning and evidence under each.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark separate description; 1 mark no developing line/judgement [2] (b) 1 mark criteria; 1 mark weighing [2]

items.stem: “Every government should publish all public contracts online.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? You may wish to consider: the perspective of Transparency International; the quality of the evidence.
items.answer: For: Corruption thrives when deals are hidden from public view. Publication allows journalists and citizens to act as watchdogs. After Ukraine introduced its ProZorro e-procurement system in 2016, many observers reported savings on public purchases. Against: Publishing contracts could reveal commercially sensitive information. The argument assumes that people will actually use published contract information to scrutinise deals. Judgement: A sustained answer weighs the evidence and reaches a qualified judgement (response to objection: sensitive details can be redacted while prices and winners are published).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–5 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (6–8 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [8]

items.stem: What is meant by “reference list” in Global Perspectives?
options: A list of all the sources cited in the text, in alphabetical order of author.
Cautious language, such as “suggests” or “may”, that avoids overstating claims.
Citing a source you have not read through another author who quotes it, e.g. (Smith, 2010, cited in Jones, 2020).
A formal, precise and objective style of writing.
items.answer: A list of all the sources cited in the text, in alphabetical order of author.
items.markingKey: Reference list: a list of all the sources cited in the text, in alphabetical order of author. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “This proves that votes at 16 could build a habit of lifelong participation.” Explain why this should be rewritten using hedging language, and rewrite it.
items.answer: One piece of evidence rarely proves a claim on a complex political issue; hedging reflects the strength of the evidence. Rewrite: “This suggests that votes at 16 could build a habit of lifelong participation.”
items.markingKey: 1 mark evidence does not prove; 1 mark hedging matches strength of evidence; 1 mark acceptable rewrite [3]

items.stem: The reference list of a report on the spread of online disinformation during elections must include works by: Petrov (2023); Silva (2019); Tanaka (2018); Ramírez (2014). Put them in the correct order for a Harvard reference list.
items.answer: Petrov (2023), Ramírez (2014), Silva (2019), Tanaka (2018).
items.markingKey: Alphabetical by first author’s surname. 2 marks fully correct; 1 mark one pair out of order [2]

items.stem: A student’s report on corruption in public procurement uses a book by T. Haddad (2019, London: Harbour Academic Press), titled “Corruption in public procurement: policy and practice”, and a journal article by Okafor and Ramírez (2013). It also uses a webpage from the UN website accessed on 3 March 2023. (a) Write the in-text citation for the journal article. (b) State two details that must be recorded for the webpage reference.
items.answer: (a) (Okafor and Ramírez, 2013) (b) URL and date accessed (also author/organisation, year, title).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that in a research report on disputes over shared rivers, academic style matters as much as content? Consider different perspectives in your answer.
items.answer: For: Precise, hedged language shows the strength of evidence accurately. Consistent referencing makes the research checkable and credible. Against: A well-styled report with weak analysis remains weak. Assessment rewards analysis, evaluation and judgement most. Judgement: Style serves content: it cannot replace strong analysis, but poor style can undermine it.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–3 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (4–6 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (7–9 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [9]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why a student researching the spread of online disinformation during elections should keep a detailed research log.
items.answer: It records decisions and reasons as they happen, so changes of direction can be explained and justified; it provides evidence for honest reflection on methods, problems and learning; it shows the work is the student’s own.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason, 1 mark each developed [4]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why a student researching the use of economic sanctions should keep a detailed research log.
items.answer: It records decisions and reasons as they happen, so changes of direction can be explained and justified; it provides evidence for honest reflection on methods, problems and learning; it shows the work is the student’s own.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason, 1 mark each developed [4]

items.stem: Extract from a student’s research reflection on migration caused by climate change: “I started with a broad question but narrowed it after my supervisor meeting. My survey response rate was very low, so I added interviews. I now realise I mainly read sources that agreed with my own view.” Identify one change of direction recorded in the reflection.
items.answer: Narrowing the question; adding interviews after a low response rate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark [1]

items.stem: “In a research report on reform of the UN Security Council, reflecting on the research process is as important as the findings.” To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Reflection develops independent research skills that transfer to university and work. It shows awareness of limitations and bias. Against: The findings answer the research question, which is the purpose of the report. Reflection without strong findings has limited value to readers. Judgement: Both matter: reflection makes the limits and strengths of the findings clear.
